title: Nosferatu

evidence.note: Published 1922; the maximum US copyright term for a pre-1923 work is 75 years, so even counting any URAA restoration for a German work still protected abroad in 1996, the term fully ran out no later than 1 January 1998. Nosferatu is public domain in the US by expiry, regardless of its German origin.

Hans Erdmann's 1922 score is public domain as a composition, but virtually every RECORDING you can obtain is a modern performance with its own copyright, and many circulating prints carry newly composed scores. Treat the audio on any copy you download as protected unless proven otherwise.

Unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) — the novel has been public domain for decades (and the Stoker estate's 1925 lawsuit famously ordered all prints of Nosferatu destroyed; the film survived through illicit copies).
The 2024 Eggers remake is an active studio property; avoid marketing that implies affiliation with it.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
The F.W. Murnau Foundation's tinted restorations are separately protected in various jurisdictions; archival scans are the free source.

editorial:
A court ordered every print of Nosferatu burned in 1925 — Bram Stoker's widow sued the unauthorized Dracula adaptation and won. The film survived through bootleg copies, outlived the novel's copyright, outlived its own, and became the most influential vampire film ever made. Today both the film and the novel it stole from are public domain in the US.

The living rights are all in the audio and the restorations: nearly every available copy carries a modern score recording or a foundation restoration. The images are free; the sound on your particular copy probably isn't.
faq: Is Nosferatu public domain even though it's German?

Yes. The maximum US copyright term for a pre-1923 work like this one is 75 years, so even with URAA factored in, the German work's hypothetical US protection ran out no later than 1 January 1998 — 1922 is safely clear by 2026.
Can I use the music from a Nosferatu Blu-ray?
Almost certainly not — modern recordings and newly composed scores are protected. Use the images and add your own audio.
